title: From Bean to Bean: Parent Guide
endLine: One bean grows, flowers, makes new beans, and completes the circle.

scenes.tts: Where do new beans come from? Grow a bean from seed to seed and watch the cycle with your child. Over about three months, your child practices looking closely, measuring each week, and checking a guess.
scenes.caption: Where do new beans come from? Grow a bean from seed to seed and watch the cycle with your child. Over about three months, your child practices looking closely, measuring each week, and checking a guess.
scenes.visual: Open on a green bean on a plate beside a dry seed and a pot on a sunny windowsill. Show the question “Where do new beans come from?” as the pot becomes the center of a five-slice timeline. The pot and timeline fill most of the frame. Keep the sunlight moving.
scenes.narration: Where do new beans come from? Grow a bean from seed to seed and watch the cycle with your child. Over about three months, your child practices looking closely, measuring each week, and checking a guess.

scenes.visual: Same sunlit windowsill workbench stays in place while sunlight motes drift slowly. Warm bold title fades in cleanly: 'From Bean to Bean' with small subtitle 'Parent Activity Guide'.

scenes.tts: Use untreated bush bean seeds. Check for bean or legume allergies. Stay with your child when handling seeds. Keep loose seeds away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Never taste the plant during the activity. Wash hands after handling soil, seeds, or plants.
scenes.caption: Use untreated bush bean seeds. Check for bean or legume allergies. Stay with your child when handling seeds. Keep loose seeds away from children under four. Call 911 if choking. Never taste the plant during the activity. Wash hands after handling soil, seeds, or plants.
scenes.visual: On the same windowsill, show an adult checking the untreated seed packet and sliding the seeds away from the edge. Brief labels read “Under 4: choking risk,” “Call 911 if choking,” and “No tasting.” End with moving soap bubbles and a handwashing drawing.
scenes.narration: Use untreated bush bean seeds. Check for bean or legume allergies. Stay with your child when handling seeds. Keep loose seeds away from children under four. Call 911 if choking. Never taste the plant during the activity. Wash hands after handling soil, seeds, or plants.

scenes.tts: Gather potting mix and two or three pots with drainage holes. Soak one extra bean overnight. Help your child peel it and split it open to find the tiny leaves. Ask, “What do you think this will become?” Then toss the soaked seed.
scenes.caption: Gather potting mix and two or three pots with drainage holes. Soak one extra bean overnight. Help your child peel it and split it open to find the tiny leaves. Ask, “What do you think this will become?” Then toss the soaked seed.
scenes.visual: At the same workbench, show a bag of potting mix and two pots with saucers. Zoom in on a soaked bean. An adult guides the child’s hands as the skin peels away and the halves open to show the tiny leaves. End with the adult dropping the soaked bean into the trash.
scenes.narration: Gather potting mix and two or three pots with drainage holes. Soak one extra bean overnight. Help your child peel it and split it open to find the tiny leaves. Ask, “What do you think this will become?” Then toss the soaked seed.

scenes.tts: Dampen the potting mix before scooping it. Fill each pot to about two centimeters below the rim. Plant two or three seeds about three centimeters deep. Cover them and water until it drips out. Date the label. Use your sunniest window or plant outside after the last spring frost. Write down your child’s sprouting guess.
scenes.caption: Dampen the potting mix before scooping it. Fill each pot to about two centimeters below the rim. Plant two or three seeds about three centimeters deep. Cover them and water until it drips out. Date the label. Use your sunniest window or plant outside after the last spring frost. Write down your child’s sprouting guess.
scenes.visual: Show the adult dampening the potting mix before scooping it. Use a pot cross-section to show the approximate soil level and planting depth. Soil covers the seeds before water drips into the saucer. A dated craft stick slides in. Show the pot moving to the sunny window and a pencil recording the child’s guess.
scenes.narration: Dampen the potting mix before scooping it. Fill each pot to about two centimeters below the rim. Plant two or three seeds about three centimeters deep. Cover them and water until it drips out. Date the label. Use your sunniest window or plant outside after the last spring frost. Write down your child’s sprouting guess.

scenes.tts: Visit together weekly for about ten to fifteen weeks. Measure the tallest plant with a ruler or with string and large blocks. Count leaves and draw the plant. Water when the soil surface feels dry. At about five centimeters, snip all but the strongest one or two yourself.
scenes.caption: Visit together weekly for about ten to fifteen weeks. Measure the tallest plant with a ruler or with string and large blocks. Count leaves and draw the plant. Water when the soil surface feels dry. At about five centimeters, snip all but the strongest one or two yourself.
scenes.visual: Show the calendar turning and the adult helping measure from the soil to the plant’s top. Show a ruler, then string beside large building blocks. Near the five-centimeter mark, the adult snips the smaller stems at soil level.
scenes.narration: Visit together weekly for about ten to fifteen weeks. Measure the tallest plant with a ruler or with string and large blocks. Count leaves and draw the plant. Water when the soil surface feels dry. At about five centimeters, snip all but the strongest one or two yourself.

scenes.tts: Before the flowers open, here is a question for you. Suppose your beans grow indoors on a sunny windowsill, with no bees at all. Will those flowers still make pods with new seeds, or stay empty?
scenes.caption: Before the flowers open, here is a question for you. Suppose your beans grow indoors on a sunny windowsill, with no bees at all. Will those flowers still make pods with new seeds, or stay empty?
scenes.visual: Same windowsill pot, now a full leafy bush bean plant with small closed white buds. The closed windowpane behind it shows an outdoor garden with a dashed crossed-out bee icon outside the glass. Bold on-screen question appears at top: 'No bees indoors: pods or empty?'
scenes.narration: Before the flowers open, here is a question for you. Suppose your beans grow indoors on a sunny windowsill, with no bees at all. Will those flowers still make pods with new seeds, or stay empty?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the windowsill plant, closed windowpane, and question 'No bees indoors: pods or empty?' stay steadily on screen. Sunlight motes drift slowly and the leafy branches sway softly while a subtle circular timer arc sweeps around the question mark.

scenes.tts: They can make pods. Bean flowers mostly pollinate themselves, often before opening. In warm weather, a hooked stem usually appears in five to fourteen days. Flowers usually open about four to seven weeks after planting. Ask your child, “What do you think will grow where the flowers are?”
scenes.caption: They can make pods. Bean flowers mostly pollinate themselves, often before opening. In warm weather, a hooked stem usually appears in five to fourteen days. Flowers usually open about four to seven weeks after planting. Ask your child, “What do you think will grow where the flowers are?”
scenes.visual: Zoom into a closed bud. Show pollen reaching the center before the flower opens, then the center growing into a pod. Use a schematic timeline with “Sprouts in warm weather” above “Usually 5–14 days,” and “Flowers” above “Usually about 4–7 weeks.”
scenes.narration: They can make pods. Bean flowers mostly pollinate themselves, often before opening. In warm weather, a hooked stem usually appears in five to fourteen days. Flowers usually open about four to seven weeks after planting. Ask your child, “What do you think will grow where the flowers are?”

scenes.tts: Tiny pods show up within a week or two of the first flowers. Green pods are ready to pick about seven to nine weeks after planting. For eating later, an adult boils picked green pods for at least thirty minutes. Leave at least three pods on the plant.
scenes.caption: Tiny pods show up within a week or two of the first flowers. Green pods are ready to pick about seven to nine weeks after planting. For eating later, an adult boils picked green pods for at least thirty minutes. Leave at least three pods on the plant.
scenes.visual: Show tiny pods growing from flowers on the same plant. Show full green pods with the label “Picking: about 7–9 weeks.” An adult takes some to a visibly bubbling pot labeled “Boil 30 minutes or more.” Three pods remain on the plant.
scenes.narration: Tiny pods show up within a week or two of the first flowers. Green pods are ready to pick about seven to nine weeks after planting. For eating later, an adult boils picked green pods for at least thirty minutes. Leave at least three pods on the plant.

scenes.tts: Over the next three to six weeks, the pods dry and the seeds rattle. Ask, “Will the new seeds look like the one we planted?” Open a dry pod together and compare its seeds with one from the packet. After the seeds ripen, the plant yellows and dies.
scenes.caption: Over the next three to six weeks, the pods dry and the seeds rattle. Ask, “Will the new seeds look like the one we planted?” Open a dry pod together and compare its seeds with one from the packet. After the seeds ripen, the plant yellows and dies.
scenes.visual: Show the remaining green pods turning yellow, then dry and papery. Show one rattling before adult and child open it together. Place a new seed beside a seed from the packet for comparison. In the background, the old plant yellows and droops.
scenes.narration: Over the next three to six weeks, the pods dry and the seeds rattle. Ask, “Will the new seeds look like the one we planted?” Open a dry pod together and compare its seeds with one from the packet. After the seeds ripen, the plant yellows and dies.

scenes.tts: Divide a paper plate into five slices. Have your child draw a seed, a sprout, a leafy plant, flowers, and a pod with seeds. Draw an arrow from the pod back to the seed. Your child practices making a guess and checking it against what they saw.
scenes.caption: Divide a paper plate into five slices. Have your child draw a seed, a sprout, a leafy plant, flowers, and a pod with seeds. Draw an arrow from the pod back to the seed. Your child practices making a guess and checking it against what they saw.
scenes.visual: Same sunlit table: the circular timeline ring from Scene 1 transforms directly into a drawn paper plate divided into five clean slices, filling in clockwise with schematic sketches—seed, sprout, leafy plant, flowers, open pod with seeds. A bold curved arrow sweeps from the pods slice back to the seed slice and pulses warmly.
